title: Acceptance criteria for progressive structured outputs with transactional tool handoffs and repair semantics
creator: Priya Nair
description: Define unambiguous acceptance criteria for progressive (incremental/streamed) structured outputs that include transactional handoffs to external "tools"/functions and an explicit, deterministic repair/compensation model for partial or out-of-order fragments. Goal: make consumer parsing and retry logic simple and predictable while enabling the runtime to perform graceful degradation and automatic repair where safe.
scope: Acceptance criteria and test cases for: (1) fragment sequencing and checkpointing tokens, (2) tool-invocation idempotency and deterministic repair paths, (3) error classification with corresponding runtime behavior, (4) observability contract and telemetry fields, (5) rollout gating rules for runtime and SDK consumers.
out_of_scope: Full implementation details of kernels, specific SDK APIs beyond required headers, non-streaming bulk export formats, and policy decisions about customer-chargeback (billing) for repair replays.
requirements: Fragments must include a stable fragment_id and sequence_index and a session_checkpoint token that can be used for resumable reads.
Tool invocations must be annotated with tool_id, invocation_id, idempotency_key, and expected_side_effects fingerprint (string).
Every streaming envelope MUST include a correlation_id that spans the entire request lifecycle (client -> runtime -> tool -> runtime -> client).

Runtime must emit one of three envelope finality markers: 'complete', 'soft_fault', or 'hard_fail'. Soft_fault indicates compensating or repair steps will be attempted; hard_fail indicates consumer must abort and surface an error.

On detection of schema drift (fragment payload schema incompatible with declared schema_version), the runtime will emit a 'schema_negotiation' fragment containing the runtime_digest and suggested_patch (string-encoded), and mark the fragment as 'repairable' for up to 30s by default.

All tool handoffs must support a deterministic repair path: if a tool invocation response is missing or partial, the runtime can re-run the invocation using the idempotency_key and attach a 'repair' fragment that reconciles divergent outputs with a conflict_resolution_strategy (e.g. prefer_runtime, prefer_tool, merge_by_key).
SDKs must provide a lightweight parser that exposes an ordered stream of typed events: fragment_received, tool_dispatched, tool_response, repair_applied, finality_marker.
acceptance_criteria: Parsing: consuming SDK or server can reassemble the full structured object by applying fragments in sequence_index order using the session_checkpoint tokens; test harness reconstructs same object for 1000 randomized fragment reorder/insertion scenarios.

Deterministic repair: when a tool response is replayed against the same idempotency_key, the system produces either the identical tool_response_id or a repair fragment that when applied yields the same final structured object; verified in integration tests with replayed traffic.

Error modes: soft_fault fragments are automatically retried for repair up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff and produce telemetry events. If all retries fail, runtime emits a final 'soft_fault' envelope with 'repair_suggestion' metadata. Hard_fail immediately emits a 'hard_fail' envelope and increments the hard_error counter.

Observability: every fragment-level event contains correlation_id, fragment_id, sequence_index, session_checkpoint, tool_id (if applicable), invocation_id, idempotency_key, retry_count, runtime_version. Telemetry ingestion shows these fields for all production canaries before full rollout.

SLO/metrics: in canary traffic, first-fragment-to-first-byte latency must be <150ms p95 and overall repair-induced latency increase must be <25% compared to baseline for the same workload. Fragment loss or unrecoverable hard_fail rate must be <0.5% across canary tenants.

Backward compatibility: clients that only consume completed-envelopes (non-streaming) must still receive a 'final full object' envelope within 5s for short-running requests; streaming clients can opt-in to early fragments via a header. Tests include legacy SDK consumers.

Security: idempotency_key and invocation_id are treated as audit fields; sensitive tool output must be redacted in telemetry per PII policy. Security review completed and signoff captured in this ticket.

Acceptance tests: automated suite with 2000 simulated users, chaos injection that drops fragments or simulates out-of-order delivery, and a set of real-customer prompts (anonymized) verifying graceful degradation and repair semantics. All tests must pass in CI and canary before merging the runtime change.
test_scenarios: Unit: fragment serializer/deserializer maintains order and honors sequence_index.
Integration: end-to-end pipeline with a mock tool that sometimes returns partial JSON; verify repair fragments resolve and final object matches golden file.
Chaos: randomly drop up to 30% of fragments during a run; ensure session_checkpoint enables successful resume and finality_marker is produced in <60s for 95% of sessions.
Idempotency: submit duplicate tool invocation with same idempotency_key across different nodes; confirm single effective side-effect and identical logical response (or acceptable repair fragment).
Backcompat: legacy SDK receives final-envelopes for non-stream consumers within 5s while streaming clients receive fragments incrementally.
monitoring_and_telemetry: Events: fragment_emitted, fragment_applied, tool_dispatched, tool_response_received, repair_attempt, finality_emitted; each includes correlation_id, fragment_id, sequence_index, session_checkpoint, runtime_version.
Metrics: fragment_loss_rate, repair_success_rate, soft_fault_rate, hard_fail_rate, p95_first_fragment_latency, median_repair_latency, canary_error_rate.
Logs: structured logs for repair decisions including conflict_resolution_strategy and pre/post-merge diffs (diffs redacted where PII).
Dashboards: per-model and per-tenant panels showing fragment loss and repair failures with linked traces to inspect replayed tool invocations.
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged release: default off. SDK header 'X-RW-Stream-Mode: progressive' opt-in for clients.
Canary stage 1: internal tenants only (dev+staging) for 48h, observe telemetry. Gates: soft_fault_rate < 1%, hard_fail_rate < 0.5%, p95_first_fragment_latency < 150ms.
Canary stage 2: 5% production traffic for 72h. Run automated repair integration tests against production traffic snapshot. If gates pass, proceed.
Wider rollout: 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 2 weeks with progressive SDK availability and documentation. Rollback if any gate breaches by >50% relative increase over baseline.
Post-rollout: 30-day observation window; run a retention job to surface any long-tail repair regressions and customer-reported parsing issues.
notes: Trade-offs discussed: storing repair state increases memory pressure per session; agreed bounded retention (default 30s) and configuration per tenant.
Decision: adopt 'repair_by_replay' as primary strategy, with conflict_resolution_strategy default 'prefer_runtime' to reduce external side-effect divergence.
Follow-up: separate ticket to enumerate SDK language bindings for event stream API and migration guide for non-streaming clients.
